steps: This video shows how a hard service level target decides an architecture before cost or quality ever do. The governance board hands you a budget of two point four million dollars over twelve months and a deadline to propose, expecting return on investment across clinical, claims and service.

Instead of building a prototype, you run a discovery workshop with the clinical team. They reply with two hard constraints: answers under three seconds during consults, and no patient health information without a signed B A A. These become non-functional gates.

You send architecture X to the S L A gate. It scores higher on quality, but averages four point two seconds. That breaks the three second limit, so the gate eliminates it. A failed gate means quality is irrelevant.
Architecture Y goes through the gate at two point one seconds and passes. Only options that survive the gates move on, and now they are compared on efficiency and solution cost.

For claims, you send the board an architecture decision record, A D R seven, proposing Enterprise with a B A A and zero data retention. It lists no alternatives, so the board sends it back marked incomplete.

You add both rejected options and say why: Pro offers no B A A, and the open source model is twelve points less accurate. You also record the cost accepted for compliance, twelve cents versus eight cents.

The board now approves A D R seven, together with requirements, success criteria and the risk register, because alternatives and trade-offs are on record. Takeaway: hard constraints act as pass or fail gates first, and only survivors compete on cost. The full walkthrough is in the Gennoor Claude certification course.
